title: The fibre functor at the geometric point is an equivalence
statement:
Fix the global finite-field datum [def-weil-finite-field-fiber], a prime $\ell\neq p$, an algebraic closure $\Qlb$ of $\Ql$, a finite extension $E/\Ql$ in $\Qlb$ with valuation ring $\mathcal O_E$ and uniformizer $\varpi_E$, and $n\geq1$; put $A_{E,n}=\mathcal O_E/\varpi_E^n$ and $s=\operatorname{Spec}k$. Each of the four fibre functors of [def-weil-finite-coefficient-point]

$$
\operatorname{Fib}_s:D^b_c(s,A_{E,n})\to D^b_{\mathrm{fin}}(A_{E,n}),\quad
\operatorname{Fib}_s:D^b_c(s,\mathcal O_E)\to D^b_{\mathrm{fg}}(\mathcal O_E),\quad
\operatorname{Fib}_s:D^b_c(s,E)\to D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E),\quad
\operatorname{Fib}_s:D^b_c(s,\Qlb)\to D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(\Qlb)
$$

is an equivalence of categories which commutes with the shifts and carries distinguished triangles to distinguished triangles. Here the source categories are those of [def-weil-finite-torsion-constructibility], [def-weil-derived-complete-integral-detailed], [def-weil-rationalization-karoubi] and [def-weil-algebraically-closed-coefficients] for $Y=s$, and the targets those of [def-weil-point-finite-cohomology-complexes], [def-weil-point-fg-complete-complexes], [def-weil-point-fd-complexes] and [def-weil-point-fd-qlbar-category].

source.place: the two displays asserting that $\operatorname{Fib}_s$ is an equivalence (moved out of the definition)

proof.text: Write $A=\mathcal O_E$, $\pi=\varpi_E$, $A_n=A/\pi^n$ and $B=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{E,s}$. The coefficient DVR theorem makes $A$ a domain with every ideal principal, hence Noetherian, and with finite residue field. Choosing a finite set of residue representatives and successively writing $x=r_0+\pi x_1$ shows that every element of $A_n$ is represented by $\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}r_j\pi^j$; thus $A_n$ is finite and Noetherian. The continuous-coefficient description, applied to the noetherian scheme $s$, identifies $\Gamma(s,B)$ canonically with $C(\{*\},A)=A$, preserving constants and all quotient projections. The completed-constant reduction theorem gives flatness of $B$ over $\underline A$ and $B\otimes^L_{\underline A}\underline{A_n}\simeq\underline{A_n}$. Indeed the resolution $[A\xrightarrow{\pi^n}A]$ of $A_n$ becomes $[B\xrightarrow{\pi^n}B]$. Constant-sheaf exactness and this flatness make its negative cohomology zero. Exactness of sections therefore gives $\Gamma(s,\underline{A_n})=A_n$, with the canonical map from constant values as the identification. No identification of $B$ with the discrete constant sheaf $\underline A$ is made.

source.place: Tags 093J and 093M, lemma-constant-exact and lemma-completion-flat; continuous coefficient identification as in Bhatt-Scholze Lemma 6.8.2

proof.text: For either $(R,\mathcal R)=(A_n,\underline{A_n})$ or $(A,B)$ define $L_{\mathcal R}(M)=\mathcal R\otimes_{\underline R}\underline M$ for an $R$-module $M$. Here constant sheaves and sheaf tensor products have exactly their existing definitions. There is an adjunction $L_{\mathcal R}\dashv\Gamma(s,-)$: a sheaf map $u:L_{\mathcal R}M\to F$ gives $m\mapsto u_s(1\otimes m)$; conversely $t:M\to F(s)$ gives, before sheafification, $b\otimes m\mapsto b\,t(m)|_U$ on every object $U$, and then extends uniquely to the sheaf tensor product. These constructions are inverse and natural; the balancing relation is precisely $R$-linearity of $t$. Constant sheafification is exact by the arbitrary-site module-sheafification theorem. Thus $L_{\underline{A_n}}$ is exact, and $L_B$ is exact by flatness in step 1. Both right adjoints are exact by the point-sections theorem. For any finitely presented $R$-module $M$, a presentation $R^a\to R^b\to M\to0$ and exactness give $\Gamma(s,L_{\mathcal R}M)\cong\operatorname{coker}(R^a\to R^b)=M$. On free generators this is $m\mapsto1\otimes m$, so the isomorphism is precisely the adjunction unit, not an arbitrary identification.

source.place: Tags 03EI and 093M; the displayed adjunction and finite-presentation calculation are written out from the sheafification and tensor definitions

proof.text: Apply the exact-functor derived factorization to the two exact adjoints in step 2. They act termwise, commute with every shift and preserve distinguished triangles. Their termwise unit and counit are chain maps; naturality makes them commute with differentials, and the two triangle identities hold degree by degree. They descend through the localization, with the same identities, to an adjunction on the unbounded derived categories. Exact-functor preservation of homology identifies the cohomology of the unit $M\to\Gamma(s,L_{\mathcal R}M)$ with the underived unit at $H^i(M)$. Consequently this derived unit is an isomorphism whenever all $H^i(M)$ are finitely presented, by the cohomological isomorphism criterion. In particular it is an isomorphism on $D^b_{\mathrm{fin}}(A_n)$ and on $D^b_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)$: finite modules over the finite Noetherian ring $A_n$, and finitely generated modules over the Noetherian ring $A$, are finitely presented. This argument uses the descended termwise unit and counit themselves, so their normalization is fixed.

source.place: Tag 015F, lemma-right-derived-exact-functor; termwise adjunction identities; homology compatibility from homology.tex Tag 010N

proof.text:
For a constructible $A_n$-module sheaf $F$ on $s_{\mathrm{proet}}$, finite-ring constructible origin gives $F\cong
u_s^*G$ with $G$ constructible on $s_{\mathrm{et}}$. Every nonempty locally closed subscheme of $s$ is $s$, since a field has no nontrivial ideals and its spectrum has one point. Thus $G$ is finite locally constant. The algebraically closed etale-point theorem identifies $G$ naturally with the constant sheaf of $G(s)$; the same isomorphism respects addition and every scalar action, by its naturality in maps of underlying sheaves. Its identity stalk is $G(s)$, and the finite-locally-constant module-values theorem explicitly turns its finite constant-value trivializations into finite geometric stalks. Hence $G(s)$ is finite. Pullback $
u_s^*$ carries constant module sheaves to constant module sheaves: both composites are left adjoint to sections, since sections of $
u_{s,*}F$ are $F(s)$ by the comparison-morphism definition; equivalently their maps send each constant value to that same value. The finite comparison unit gives $G(s)\cong(
u_s^*G)(s)=F(s)$. It follows that the canonical evaluation counit $\underline{F(s)}	o F$ is an isomorphism. Conversely a constant finite module sheaf is locally constant and has finite geometric stalks by the constant-stalk theorem, so is constructible. In particular sections detect zero sheaves within this constructible subcategory.

source.place: Tags 09AK and 099Y, constructible and finite locally constant comparison; etale-cohomology.tex Tag 03P5 for the geometric point

proof.text: For $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{fin}}(A_n)$, exactness of $L_{\underline{A_n}}$ identifies its cohomology sheaves with the constant finite modules $\underline{H^i(M)}$; these vanish outside a finite interval and are constructible by step 4. Thus $L_{\underline{A_n}}M\in D^b_c(s,A_n)$. Conversely sections have the asserted target by point-sections finiteness. For $K\in D^b_c(s,A_n)$, the cohomology maps of the derived counit $L_{\underline{A_n}}\Gamma(s,K)\to K$ are exactly the evaluation counits of its cohomology sheaves, by exact-functor homology compatibility. Step 4 makes them isomorphisms, and the derived isomorphism criterion makes this counit an isomorphism. Together with the unit in step 3 this proves the torsion equivalence. It also proves the detection statement used below: a bounded constructible torsion complex with zero section complex is zero. Its exactness and shift compatibility are already those of termwise sections in the point-sections theorem.

source.place: first functor in the first equivalence display; explicit adjunction proof using steps 1-4

proof.text: Every bounded $A$-complex with finitely generated cohomology is perfect. To verify the needed hypotheses explicitly, take a finitely generated module $N$. The Noetherian finite-free-resolution theorem gives $A^{r_1}\to A^{r_0}\to N\to0$. Its kernel $J\subset A^{r_0}$ is finitely generated, being the image of the first finite free term, and is torsion free because $A$ is a domain and $A^{r_0}$ is torsion free. The finite torsion-free DVR theorem makes $J$ finite free. Thus $0\to J\to A^{r_0}\to N\to0$ is a bounded finite-free resolution. The perfect-cohomology assembly theorem now gives a bounded finite-projective representative $Q$ for every $M\in D^b_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)$. The argument includes $N=0$ and does not impose finite Tor dimension on modules over $A_n$; those rings may be singular.

For any bounded finite-projective $A$-complex $Q$, $L_BQ=B\otimes_{\underline A}\underline Q$ is in $D^b_c(s,A)$ by the integral stratified-perfect characterization, using its explicit comparison with the category of derived-complete integral coefficients in the statement. Its hypotheses hold: $s$ is noetherian, of dimension zero, and $\ell$ is invertible in $k$ because $\ell\ne p$; use the single stratum $s$ and the identity trivializing cover. This is its condition (ii), with the specified completed sheaf $B$. In particular this assertion includes completeness and the reductions required in the present definition, rather than silently identifying two integral categories. The reduction calculation of step 1 also gives $L_BQ\otimes_B^L\underline{A_n}\cong\underline{Q\otimes_A A_n}$: for a finite projective term take a direct summand of a finite free term and use the same quotient map. These reductions have bounded finite cohomology in the fixed term interval of $Q$, independent of $n$. Thus step 6 shows $L_B$ carries every object of $D^b_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)$ into the integral source. Point-sections finiteness carries the integral source into $D^b_{\mathrm{fg}}(A)$. The adjunction of step 3 therefore restricts to these full subcategories, and its unit is an isomorphism there.

source.place: Definition 6.5.1 and Propositions 6.6.11, 6.8.11(3), as specialized and compared in the cited characterization; sites-modules.tex Tag 093M for the explicit reductions

proof.text: Sections are conservative on the integral source as well. If $C\in D^b_c(s,A)$ and $\Gamma(s,C)=0$, compute its $n$-th reduction using the finite free resolution $[B\xrightarrow{\pi^n}B]\to\underline{A_n}$ from step 1. Tensoring this resolution with a K-flat representative of $C$ gives the cone of multiplication by $\pi^n$; the K-flat property ensures that tensoring the resolution quasi-isomorphism remains a quasi-isomorphism. Hence, after restriction of scalars, $C\xrightarrow{\pi^n}C\to C_n\to C[1]$ is distinguished. Exact sections show $\Gamma(s,C_n)=0$. Its actual $A_n$-coefficient reduction is bounded constructible by the integral definition, so step 5 makes it zero (forgetting its scalar structure does not change its cohomology). All reductions of $C$ therefore vanish. Its derived-completeness Roos triangle is $C\to0\to0\to C[1]$, so $C=0$, for example by the long exact cohomology sequence and the cohomological isomorphism criterion. For arbitrary integral $K$, form the cone $C$ of the restricted counit $L_B\Gamma(s,K)\to K$. It is in the integral source by its triangulated-subcategory theorem. Applying sections makes this counit an isomorphism by the unit isomorphism and the adjunction triangle identity; thus $\Gamma(s,C)=0$. The preceding argument gives $C=0$, hence the counit is an isomorphism. This proves the integral equivalence, with the exactness and shift comparisons of sections.

source.place: second functor in the first display; reduction argument using sites-modules.tex Tag 093M and the prescribed completeness Roos triangle

proof.text: For the rational stage first check full faithfulness for the specified raw localization. Put $M=\Gamma(s,K)$, $N=\Gamma(s,K')$ for integral objects. The integral equivalence is $A$-linear: all its maps above are maps of $A$-modules and the section action is the canonical one. Thus it identifies $\operatorname{Hom}(K,K')$ with $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(A)}(M,N)$ as $A$-modules. Both $M,N$ are perfect by step 6. Apply perfect RHom base change to $A\to E$ and the first argument $M$. Here $E=A[1/\pi]$ by the uniformizer localization theorem and is flat by localization flatness. Consequently taking $H^0$ of that base-change isomorphism, using flat-tensor exactness, gives the canonical bijection $\operatorname{Hom}_{D(A)}(M,N)\otimes_AE\cong\operatorname{Hom}_{D(E)}(M\otimes_AE,N\otimes_AE)$. The identification $H^0(R\operatorname{Hom}(M,N))=\operatorname{Hom}_{D(A)}(M,N)$ is precisely the K-injective Hom-complex theorem applied on the one-object ringed site (and likewise for $E$). The base-change theorem specifies its map to be the scalar extension of the functor-induced Hom map; hence this bijection sends $f\otimes a$ to $a(f\otimes E)$, exactly the morphism map defining the rational fibre functor. The rationalization definition gives the left-hand Hom groups, so this proves full faithfulness without adjoining idempotents.

source.place: Tag 0A6A, lemma-base-change-RHom (1), with its preceding canonical-map construction; algebra.tex Tag 00HT

proof.text: For $V\in D^b_{\mathrm{fd}}(E)$ choose a representing complex. For each of its finitely many nonzero $H^i(V)$ choose a finite basis and lift each basis vector to a cycle in degree $i$. The basis theorem supplies these bases; the lifts exist by the definition of cohomology as cycles modulo boundaries. Sending the standard basis in degree $i$ to these cycles defines a chain map from the zero-differential bounded finite free complex $P_E=\bigoplus_iE^{d_i}[-i]$ to the representative of $V$. It induces the chosen isomorphism on every cohomology module, so is a quasi-isomorphism. Let $P_A=\bigoplus_iA^{d_i}[-i]$ with zero differential. Step 7 puts $L_BP_A$ in the integral source, and step 3 identifies its sections with $P_A$; after rationalization its image is $P_E\cong V$. This proves essential surjectivity, including $V=0$ by the empty sum. The rational functor commutes with shifts and preserves distinguished triangles: sections does so, and flat tensoring with $E$ is an exact functor and hence has the exact derived factorization. Every distinguished triangle in the raw rationalization is isomorphic to an image of an integral distinguished triangle by its definition. Thus the specified rational fibre functor is an exact equivalence.

source.place: third functor in the first equivalence display; explicit finite-basis cycle lift and integral lattice

proof.text: For source objects $(E,K)$ and $(E',K')$ in the common-stage category, a morphism is represented over a finite common field $L$. The scalar-extension comparison $\varphi_{L/E}$ identifies its image under the fibre functor with conjugation by the canonical comparisons at $E$ and $E'$. At each common field $L$, Steps 9–10 give the rational fibre equivalence and hence a bijection on the represented Hom groups. The identity and three-field composition equations in the section scalar-extension theorem make these bijections compatible with all transition maps.

source.place: final display asserting the common-stage Qlbar equivalence

proof.text: The directed-colimit statement [def-weil-directed-colimit-abelian-groups] gives representatives and equality after passage to a common later stage for exactly these abelian-group Hom colimits. A target representative lifts through the rational Hom bijection at its stage. If two images agree, they agree at a common later stage; compatibility from Step 11 and injectivity at that stage make the original representatives agree there. Thus the Hom-colimit map is bijective. A target object $(E,V)$ has a preimage $(E,K)$ by Step 10 at the same field $E$. Hence the common-stage functor is fully faithful and essentially surjective.

source.place: final display asserting the common-stage Qlbar equivalence

proof.text: The section scalar-extension theorem defines $\varphi_{L/E,K}=(\Gamma(s,\chi_{L/E,K})\circ\theta_{L/E,K})^{-1}$. The completion comparison commutes with every integer shift by [lem-weil-point-completed-scalar-shift], and the sections-tensor comparison does so by [lem-weil-point-sections-tensor-shift]. Exact termwise sections preserves the first equality, so the composite and its inverse commute with the specified shifts. Tensoring with $L$ preserves that equality at the rational stage. Naturality and the scalar-extension theorem's identity and three-field equations make it compatible with the common-stage transition maps. Thus the common-stage fibre functor commutes with shifts.

source.place: final display asserting the common-stage Qlbar equivalence

proof.text: Finally, every distinguished source triangle in the common-stage category is represented at one finite stage. The rational fibre functor is exact at that stage by Step 10, and the scalar comparisons at the three vertices and the last shifted arrow are compatible by Step 13. Hence the image triangle is distinguished in the target common-stage category. This proves the fourth equivalence, with the exact shifts and triangles specified in the statement.

source.place: final display asserting the common-stage Qlbar equivalence
